top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) answers a first-order question, who gains and loses when technology and trade shift labour demand, with a framework for why the wage structure moves and design-based evidence on where and how slowly adjustment happens. The core work is mature: more than a decade of replication and critique has refined magnitudes and persistence without overturning the finding of slow, concentrated, costly adjustment. The citation can be worded around labour demand, wages and local labour markets, which avoids claiming the task model and limits overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes. The main costs are Dorn's exclusion and the one-or-two-achievements question; I would prefer Autor, Dorn and Hanson under an import-competition citation, but that is not on the slate. P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) has the cleaner attribution and is mature, but its quantitative importance is identified indirectly and the 2022 overlap would need explaining, so it ranks second. Either is preferable to no award.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. No co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz, Dorn, Kiyotaki or Moore. B027 is adjacent to my field of empirical labour economics, and I presented the 2021 prize, which may make me more alert to overlap. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
